title: Except the fear of heaven (Berakhot 33b)
hookLine: everything is in heaven's hands except the fear of heaven
tomorrow: a long prayer or a short one: which does a scared family need?

cards: The night before surgery, the family gets a call: be there by six, nothing to eat after midnight, the doctor will explain the risks. Every line of it is about things no one in the family controls.

The Talmud has a sentence for that list. Rabbi Chanina says: everything is in the hands of heaven, except the fear of heaven. Then it proves it with a verse, and the verse makes the whole thing sound small.

teach.b: Here's the verse, Moses speaking in Deuteronomy: "what doth the LORD thy God require of thee, but to fear the LORD thy God." Only that? As if awe were a light errand.
The Talmud notices, and asks it straight: is the fear of heaven a small thing? Its answer is honest.
Yes, for Moses it was small. Then a parable.
Someone asked for a big vessel he already owns: it feels small to him. Asked for a small one he doesn't own, it feels huge. Moses had awe, so asking for it sounded easy.

For the rest of us it's the big vessel we haven't got yet. Fear of heaven, yirat shamayim, here sits closer to awe than to terror: living as if God is really there. And notice what the line hands you.
The weather, the diagnosis, the surgeon's steady hands: heaven's.

teach.h: THE ONE THING LEFT WITH YOU.
teach.b: How you stand inside all that, whether you meet it with reverence or let it go flat, Rabbi Chanina leaves with you.
The one thing that's yours is not small. It's the hardest thing on the list, and it can't be done for you.

how: Yirat shamayim, fear or awe of heaven, is a phrase Jews use for a person's reverence for God; Rabbi Chanina's line, 'everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven,' is often quoted when people talk about free choice.

games.q: what does “except the fear of heaven” mean?
o: a blessing said when you look up at the open sky
your own awe is the one thing heaven leaves you to choose
fear God, since heaven decides what happens to everyone

games.q: the puzzle, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: what does God ask, but to fear
the big vessel you don't own

s: 'fear of heaven' here means being terrified of God
it sits closer to awe and reverence: living as if God is really there.
the Talmud admits awe is small only for someone like Moses
is the fear of heaven a small thing? yes, for Moses.
Rabbi Chanina's line means people control what happens to them
everything is in heaven's hands except the fear of heaven.

games.q: your team loses the final on a bad call. on the bus home, everyone is either raging at the ref or scrolling in silence. what does Rabbi Chanina's line leave in your hands?
o: nothing: the call was out of your control, so how you react is too.
how you meet it: whether you carry it with some reverence or let it go flat.
the result: if you'd wanted it more, heaven would have given it to you.
games.why: everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven. the call isn't yours; the way you stand inside it is.

practice: Pick up one ordinary object near you: a cup, a leaf, your own hand. Look at it for the whole sit as if you had never seen one before. That attention is the part no one can choose for you.

wordCard.voice: Except the fear of heaven. Everything is in heaven's hands but your own awe, which the Talmud says only felt small to Moses.

orig.note: Hebrew: fear (awe) of heaven; 'heaven' here is a way of saying God.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: awe is yours to choose, even when nothing else is. Twenty-seven of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 33b (Rabbi Chanina: everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven; is fear a small thing? for Moses, yes; the parable of the vessels)
